## Introduction

This project uses the tablet manufacturing dataset introduced in ST 558
Project 2. The data contain 4,850 tablet records from 52 compression lots
across three strengths: Low, Mid, and High. Records come from two
engineering studies and one registration campaign.

Available measurements include tablet weight, thickness, and hardness
(tablet breaking force). Measurement availability varies across records,
so missing values will be reviewed before selecting the modeling data.

This analysis will compare a tree model and a random forest for a selected
prediction task. The selected model will then be made available through
an API running in a Docker container.

## Data Import and Preparation

```{r}
# I load readxl to import the original Excel workbook.
library(readxl)

# I read the data worksheet without filtering the records.
tablet_data <- read_excel(
  "data/tablet_ipc_deidentified.xlsx",
  sheet = "data"
)

# I check the dataset dimensions and variable names.
dim(tablet_data)
names(tablet_data)
```

### Missing-value review

Before preparing the modeling dataset, I check missing values in the
response and the four candidate predictors. I also identify which
studies and strengths have missing target hardness values.

```{r}
# I load dplyr to filter, group, and summarize records.
library(dplyr)

# I count missing values in the response and candidate predictors.
missing_counts <- data.frame(
  variable = c(
    "hardness_kp",
    "strength",
    "target_hardness_kp",
    "sampling_point",
    "speed_setting"
  ),
  missing_records = c(
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$hardness_kp)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$strength)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$target_hardness_kp)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$sampling_point)),
    sum(is.na(tablet_data$speed_setting))
  )
)

missing_counts
```

I summarize records with missing target hardness by study and strength
to understand where these missing values occur.

```{r}
# I count records with missing target hardness within each group.
tablet_data |>
  filter(is.na(target_hardness_kp)) |>
  group_by(study, strength) |>
  summarize(
    missing_targets = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

Of the 4,850 source records, 1,950 lack a measured hardness value,
leaving 2,900 records with an observed response. Strength, sampling
point, and speed setting have no missing values. Target hardness
is missing in 1,240 records, all from the Registration study.
These findings will guide the preparation of the modeling dataset.

### Preparing the modeling dataset

I restore missing Registration target hardness values using the
predefined settings documented in Project 2: 4 kp for Low strength
and 7 kp for Mid and High strengths. Existing targets are retained.
These values come from documented manufacturing settings rather
than estimates calculated from measured hardness.

I store the prepared records separately from the original imported
data. Strength, sampling point, and speed setting are represented
as categorical variables using factors.

```{r}
# I create a prepared copy of the imported data.
prepared_data <- tablet_data |>
  mutate(

    # I restore missing Registration targets using the
    # predefined values and retain existing targets.
    target_hardness_kp = ifelse(
      study == "Registration" & is.na(target_hardness_kp),
      ifelse(strength == "Low", 4, 7),
      target_hardness_kp
    ),

    # I represent the three strengths as categories.
    strength = factor(
      strength,
      levels = c("Low", "Mid", "High")
    ),

    # I specify the sampling categories in process order.
    sampling_point = factor(
      sampling_point,
      levels = c("Pre-Start", "Beginning", "Middle", "End")
    ),

    # I represent each speed configuration as a category.
    speed_setting = factor(speed_setting)
  )

# I retain records with an observed hardness response.
# I keep the response, four predictors, and tracking columns.
model_data <- prepared_data |>
  filter(!is.na(hardness_kp)) |>
  select(
    tablet_id,
    study,
    blend,
    lot,
    sample_id,
    hardness_kp,
    strength,
    target_hardness_kp,
    sampling_point,
    speed_setting
  )
```

Records without measured hardness are excluded because an observed
response is needed for model fitting and evaluation. Study, blend,
lot, sample, and record identifiers are retained for tracking and
reviewing the data structure. The model formulas will explicitly
specify the four selected predictors.

```{r}
# I document the number of records at each preparation stage.
data.frame(
  stage = c("Imported", "Prepared", "Modeling"),
  records = c(
    nrow(tablet_data),
    nrow(prepared_data),
    nrow(model_data)
  )
)

# I check the dimensions and remaining missing values.
dim(model_data)
sum(is.na(model_data))

# I inspect the variable types.
str(model_data)

# I check representation of each strength.
model_data |>
  group_by(strength) |>
  summarize(
    records = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Prediction Goal and Predictors

I will compare a regression tree and a random forest for predicting
measured hardness for an individual tablet. The response variable is
`hardness_kp`, which records tablet breaking force in kiloponds (kp).

The initial prediction question is: How accurately can tablet hardness
be predicted using tablet strength, target hardness, sampling point,
and speed setting?

The following four variables will be considered as predictors:

| Predictor | Meaning | Reason for inclusion |
|---|---|---|
| `strength` | Low, Mid, or High tablet strength | The strengths have different tablet characteristics and intended hardness levels. |
| `target_hardness_kp` | Intended hardness setpoint | The intended hardness may help explain the measured breaking force. |
| `sampling_point` | Pre-Start, Beginning, Middle, or End | Hardness may vary across the compression run. |
| `speed_setting` | Nominal setting or turret/feeder speed combination | Operating speed may be associated with differences in measured hardness. |

Target hardness is the intended setpoint, distinct from the measured
hardness response. Missing Registration targets are restored using
the documented presets described in the data preparation section.

## Evaluation Metric

I will use root mean squared error (RMSE) as the primary metric for
tuning and comparing the models. RMSE measures prediction error in
the same units as the response, so the results can be interpreted
in kiloponds.

RMSE gives greater weight to larger prediction errors. I chose this
metric because substantial errors in predicted tablet hardness are
particularly undesirable for this prediction task. Lower RMSE
indicates better predictive performance.
